entries.title: Party Invite Phishing Scams Are the New Missed Connections
entries.summary: Email scams that look like an Evite or Paperless Post invitation are meant to snatch your data. For some, they've become an excuse to reconnect with old friends or flames.
entries.content:
This past April, while attending his nephew’s bar mitzvah on Cape Cod, Eric Umansky woke up to an inbox full of emails from people from his past. They all wanted to know the same thing: Was he actually throwing a party Saturday night?

The New York–based journalist wasn’t sure what party they were referring to, or why random acquaintances he’d met in passing 15 years ago were emailing him. On deadline and already stressed about work, he checked his phone, where more messages inquired about a supposed Paperless Post invite he’d sent for a “Special Private Dinner Party” at 7 pm on May 2.

Except Umansky hadn't sent the invite, and he wasn’t planning to host a party anytime soon.

As it turned out, he was an early victim of an email scam that has since become more widespread. What Umansky didn’t expect was the positive effect it would have on his social life.

In May, after receiving increased reports, the Federal Trade Commission issued a consumer alert warning about scammers sending “unexpected messages that look like they’re from well-known invitation platforms like Evite or Paperless Post,” noting how some messages “make you enter your email username and password to see event details” while others “tell you to enter a phone number and share a special code to RSVP.”

Umansky wasn’t sure how it happened; he thought he'd taken the necessary precautions to safeguard his email, including using two-factor authentication. All he could think to do was post a message on Facebook, LinkedIn, and his other social networks to notify people that he was, in fact, not having a party and, more importantly, “don’t come to my house.”

Phishing scams, which have proliferated across the last two decades, remain one of the biggest security risks faced both by individuals and companies. Email scams, in particular, can now be highly sophisticated, incorporating social engineering techniques like creating urgency or fear in a target and even leveraging the personal relationships between two people to manipulate a victim, what’s known as “spear phishing.” AI has only made those deceptions harder to weed out.

But in some recent cases, like Umansky’s, the fake party invite is having an unintended outcome: It is encouraging people to check in to see whether the message was actually real and, in doing so, has reignited dormant relationships.

“It was so striking to me after it happened that I actually had a thought that I was like, ‘Oh, is this a net positive?’” says Umansky, who over the last several months has reconnected with a handful of old friends and colleagues over lunch and via text. He recently spent an hour on Zoom with a former coworker who now lives in Mexico City. They hadn’t talked to each other in over a decade. “I was like, Oh, you know, I actually want to catch up with you about something. There was an idea I wanted to bat around with him, which we talked about for maybe 10 minutes. The rest of the time we talked about our lives.”

According to a 2024 study published in the scientific journal Communications Psychology examining social withdrawal, which surveyed 2,400 adults in the US, UK, and Canada, people are sometimes unwilling to contact old friends because they believe the other person won’t want to hear from them or they fear the interaction will be awkward. The research noted that “high priority placed on work and productivity in North America has led people to cut back on social connections and social time to meet increasing demands at work,” in addition to other life transitions, such as parenthood or moving to a new city.

But a suspicious party invite is exactly the kind of low-stakes incentive that has made initiating contact easier because it represents the one thing we all crave: a sense of belonging.

According to Lara Aknin, a professor of psychology at Simon Fraser University whose research has explored the hesitancy around reconnecting with lapsed contacts, only 30 percent of people actually check in with an old friend “even when we make doing so as easy as possible by helping them identify a desirable, feasible, and low-risk contact.”

With email scams, “people are motivated and willing to reach out to an old friend because the scam provides a legitimate excuse or social cover to do so,” she says. “In fact, people may even be slightly grateful for the reconnection opportunity this context affords, even though they hope the scam is false.”

Most people will only have a small number of close relationships in their lifetime, and it is even fewer these days; nearly half of the population (44 percent) have five or fewer acquaintances. “In the course of [scammers] taking advantage of that real desire, they are actually helping fill it,” Umansky says.

He’s not the only one who has reignited old relationships after being targeted by a scam. “I heard from a friend of more than 30 years,” Larry Persily wrote in the Wrangell Sentinel, a local newspaper in Alaska, of the trend. One source confirms with WIRED that they are back in touch with an ex they haven’t spoken to in years after receiving a fake invite.

To be clear, the unintended consequence of scam attempts may be reconnecting with lost friends, but they’re not all Zoom reunions and brunch. The FBI estimates that scammers tricked Americans out of $21 billion in 2025 alone, with help from AI.

Some of us remain impervious to the lure of the phishing trap invite. In late August, I received an unexpected Paperless Post invite—“Raise a Glass! Dinner & Drinks” the subject line read—from an acquaintance I hadn’t spoken to since 2017, though I immediately deleted it because I could barely remember who he was or why we even exchanged emails. I probably should have reached out. Maybe we both would’ve enjoyed the catch-up.

entries.title: ‘Primetime’ Exposes the Ego-Driven Core of Vigilante Pedophile Hunting
entries.summary: Lance Oppenheim’s new film doesn’t paint Chris Hansen as a hero. The To Catch a Predator host's real-world copycats are even more reckless.
entries.content:
Child predators are arguably the most reviled demographic in society.

So when someone like Chris Hansen, the former NBC Dateline journalist and host of the To Catch a Predator series, decides to take up the mantle of exposing them to the public, he is naturally praised as a hero.

But, as is revealed in Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime—a dramatized snapshot of Hansen’s life at the show’s peak—it’s not as simple as that. Exposing allegedly bad people for public entertainment brings up a lot of ethical concerns and unintended consequences. And while many of the vigilantes carrying out these sting operations claim they are doing a public service, their motivations become a lot more suspect when fame and money are involved.

To Catch a Predator launched in 2004. In the show, Hansen’s team would pair up with civilian watchdog group Perverted Justice, using adult “decoys” to pose as minors online and exchange messages with men in chatrooms and private DMs. After the conversations became sexual, the crew would set up a sting, inviting these men to a home to meet the decoy, only to have Hansen confront them, uttering his catchphrase, “Have a seat.” The men were technically free to leave instead of sitting for an on-camera interview, but often police were waiting outside to arrest them.

The show developed an intense fandom that remains active to this day in subreddits like r/tcap, which has 52,000 weekly visitors, despite the fact that NBC stopped airing the original series in 2007.

In A24's Primetime, a darkly told character study in theaters September 25, Hansen (Robert Pattinson) clearly enjoys the praise and seems desperate for more accolades. He brags to his two young sons that he’s about to be on prime-time television, despite them not understanding the importance of that, and complains that the show has “never won an Emmy or any of the significance it deserves.” When a fan recognizes Hansen on a flight and becomes bloodthirsty, asking the TV host if he ever wants to “bleed” the predators he’s outing, Hansen smiles and admits that what he does by disgracing them on national television is “a little worse.”

In real life, Hansen cofounded the streaming service Trublu in November 2022, where he continues his investigations into alleged child predators. But these days, he’s far from alone. His work has inspired copycats, who thrive on social media and streaming platforms like YouTube, Kick, and Facebook. These groups and individuals are largely disorganized, and as such, hard to track, but a 2022 Washington Post investigation identified at least 160 in the US. Arguably, the people running these operations are more reckless, in part because they’re driven by virality.

One of them, who goes by Skeet Hansen, was featured in the 2025 MTV documentary Predators, about the Dateline show. In the film, directed by David Osit, Skeet Hansen responds to the criticism of the movement by saying, “There’s never been a detective that solved a murder that didn't get paid for it. So why shouldn't I be able to monetize off of catching these guys like the original show and making this content for people’s entertainment?”

One of many issues with that argument is that these hunters aren’t professional investigators—and sometimes they get things wrong.

In April, YouTuber and Kick streamer Vitaly Zdorovetskiy apologized after publicly—and wrongly— accosting a man of Indian descent. He accused the man of wanting to “rape a 16-year-old” in a mock Indian accent and called him “Mr. Mumbai.” In March 2025, The New York Times reported that Zdorovetskiy’s tactics for ambushing suspected creeps included beating some of them up, dressing like the Joker; the Times piece found that there have been more than 170 violent vigilante attacks by predator-hunting groups since 2023.

I spent over a year investigating similar groups in Canada for Vice, starting in 2015, and found that some of the people being targeted in stings had severe intellectual and physical disabilities.

Law enforcement groups, meanwhile, have repeatedly denounced vigilantes, noting that their evidence often can’t be used within the criminal justice system and that confronting alleged pedophiles can allow the targeted person to escape before police can step in. In some cases, the so-called predator hunters have ended up being charged with child-porn offenses themselves.

Warning: The following contains spoilers for Primetime.

In Primetime, the catastrophic consequences of these rogue busts culminate in a sting taking down Louis William “Bill” Conradt Jr., a chief felony assistant district attorney in Rockwall County, Texas. Conradt doesn’t agree to come to a decoy house, so both the TV crew and police show up at his home, where he shoots and kills himself. (The real-life Hansen told the Hollywood Reporter he doesn’t regret the November 2006 sting. Neither he nor NBC responded to a request for comment for this story.)

There are no heroes in Primetime, and the movie doesn’t wrap up any of these threads neatly.

At the end, struggling actor “Decoy Dan,” played excellently by Skyler Gisondo, finally gets career validation when his appearances on the show earn him a SAG-AFTRA card, but it’s clear from his expression that he’s not comfortable with what he had to do to get it.

Meanwhile, Hansen’s character, who repeats the phrase “What would have happened if I wasn’t here?” to suspected predators throughout the film, leaves the audience to grapple with that question. The answers are far from black-and-white.

entries.title: How to Record Your Screen on Any Phone
entries.summary: The built-in tools on your phone—as well as some inexpensive apps—let you share whatever you’re doing with others.
entries.content:
There are numerous reasons why you might want to record what’s happening on your phone. Maybe you’re having a problem with an app and you want to share what’s going wrong with a tech-savvy friend; or maybe you're the tech-savvy friend, and you want to show someone else how to fix a bug.

Perhaps you’re starting up a YouTube channel of smartphone tutorials. Or it could be that you want to capture evidence of a new high score in a mobile game—not just a screenshot of it, but the actual act of you achieving it.

For these reasons and more, screen recordings are useful, and they’re not difficult to capture no matter what the make and model of your handset. You’ll find instructions below for the two most well-known Android phone brands, and the iPhone.

Record Your Screen on a Google Pixel

If your phone of choice is the Google Pixel, unlock your handset then swipe down from the top of the screen with two fingers to bring up the full Quick Settings selection. You should see a widget for Screen recorder—if you can’t see it, try swiping left or right. If you still can’t see it, tap the pen icon (lower right) to add it to the Quick Settings menu.

Next you’ll see a panel of toggle switches: These options let you choose whether or not the screen touches are visible in the recording, and whether you want the selfie camera feed to be visible as an overlay (handy if you’re narrating or reacting to what’s on screen). You can also opt to include audio from your phone’s apps or from the microphone.

The drop-down menu at the top lets you decide between recording the entire screen or just a single app. When you’re happy, tap Start. You’ll see a short countdown, then the recording begins. To end the recording, tap the red recording timer in the status bar at the top, then Stop. The video will be saved to Google Photos.

Record Your Screen on a Samsung Galaxy

On Samsung Galaxy phones, the process is similar but not quite identical to screen recording on a Pixel. With your phone unlocked, swipe down from the top of the display, then swipe down again on the central pane (with icons for features including Wi-Fi and the flashlight) to reveal the Screen recorder icon.

This brings up a settings panel. You can choose between Full screen and Partial screen for your recording, and there are three options for audio: None, Media (whatever your phone is playing), and Media and mic (whatever your phone is playing plus the microphone input). There’s also a toggle switch for showing taps and touches on screen.

When you’re good to go, tap Start recording. You get a short countdown, and then the recording begins—up in the corner of the screen you’ll see a widget overlay for adding annotations or a selfie camera overlay, and for pausing or stopping the recording. When you tap the stop button, the video is saved in Samsung Gallery and (if you’ve got it installed) Google Photos.

Record Your Screen on an iPhone

For iOS, the screen recorder is launched by swiping down from the top right corner of the display, then tapping the screen recorder button (it’s a circle with another circle outside it). If the icon has been removed from the Control Center somehow, tap the + (plus) button in the top left corner to add it back.

You can either tap the record button once to start the countdown and launch the recording, or press and hold the record button to choose a different app for the recording besides the default Photos option—so you can use this to broadcast your recording to Facebook or WhatsApp for example.

Pressing and holding on the record button also lets you choose whether or not to include the iPhone mic audio. (The iPhone’s native output audio is always included.) To stop the recording, tap the recording indicator at the top of the screen, then the red stop button. You’ll find your saved video stored in the Photos app.

Third-Party Screen Recording Apps

It’s worth noting that iOS restricts what third-party apps can do in terms of screen recordings, for security and privacy reasons. Most apps in this category in the Apple App Store simply tap into the iPhone’s own recording capabilities, though Record It! is worth a look if you want to add commentaries and selfie cam reactions—you just need to add these after the main recording. Clips over three minutes require the $6 Pro purchase.

On Android, there are fewer limits on what apps can do. AZ Recorder has been a popular choice for years, giving you one-tap recording options, a choice of video quality settings, and some basic editing options included as well. To remove the ads in the app and the watermarks on your exported videos, you can pay $4.49 a month for the Pro version.

Mobizen Screen Recorder is another of the leading screen recorders on Android, and comes with a similar set of features as AZ Recorder: A widget overlay for instantly starting recordings, editing tools, and a few options for video quality (both resolution and refresh rate). Again, payment is required to remove the ads and watermarks—that will set you back $3.35 a month.

entries.title: Who Killed Paulina Borsook’s Career?
entries.summary: A quarter-century ago, Borsook published a wildly prophetic, penetrating book about Silicon Valley called Cyberselfish. Then she disappeared.
entries.content:
The offers had come in earlier that day. Paulina Borsook, 72, allowed herself a flash of excitement before returning to the question of what had ruined her life.

“I don’t know what to make of it,” she said as we drove to lunch. I’d picked Borsook up outside her home near Oakland, California, a basement unit that she calls “Ice Station Zebra” on account of the cold and the color scheme and the isolation. At least that’s how I was encouraged to picture it. Borsook didn’t want me to come inside, lest I pull the old magazine hack’s scam of investing the decor with symbolic significance. She wrote enough stories of this kind in her heyday, back when she was landing bylines in WIRED and the like, to know how the game gets played. Later, she explained over email: “this place i ended up in reflects me not at all. i lost all i owned when i couldnt pay for storage and this place is the best i could find that worked with my disabilities. so i feel it REALLY doesnt reflect me/my taste/my preferences. shame and aversion.”

What had happened to Paulina Borsook? The question was haunting her, even on a day when she’d gotten such good news. It’s haunted her for a quarter-century now. In 2000, after years writing about Silicon Valley, she published a book, Cyberselfish, that discerned within the tech utopianism of the era a dead-eyed, woman-hating social malevolence—what the subtitle called the “Terribly Libertarian Culture of High-Tech.” It was smart at a moment when the whole of the tech industry had gone dumb, and it was funny where Silicon Valley was at its most self-serious. Cyberselfish got warm, if occasionally baffled, reviews. It sold something like 5,000 copies in hardcover and another 2,000 in paperback, a respectable mid-list number, no blockbuster but not a dog, either.

And then … nothing. Editors stopped taking her calls. No fellowships materialized, no second book deal, no regular MSNBC spots for the dotcom Cassandra of the boom times. Borsook couldn’t get work. She began to wonder if she had been blacklisted. Her health, always wobbly, only worsened. She was living in other people’s houses. She went broke, a process she likened to a fire in which everything burns to the ground, and was getting by on a GoFundMe and support from friends. She’d taken to calling the book TDB. That damn book.

When Borsook and I first met, in December of last year, she was fully in the midst of what she terms “this resuscitation thing.” It had happened so quickly and altogether without her knowledge: a social media post here, another one over there, celebrated tech critics like Gil Durán of The Nerd Reich exhuming her book and waving it around as proof that, even in the go-go days of the dotcom bubble, some people saw where things were headed. “Instead of centering men who missed the boat (and still don’t seem to get it), let’s lift up the work of Paulina Borsook, who saw it all very clearly and tried to warn us 25 years ago,” Durán wrote in a widely shared post on Bluesky—in response to a 2025 WIRED essay by Steven Levy. Borsook was christened a prophet, unappreciated in her time but uniquely fitted to ours. Hadn’t she written of “testosterone-poisoned guys with chips on their shoulders and too much time on their hands” years before the manosphere? Hadn’t she recuperated the Luddites as “early protesters of de-skilling” back when “Luddite” was an epithet? Hadn’t she raised her eyebrows at the theorists of Sand Hill Road playing footsie with eugenics? Cyberselfish became a minor phenomenon without Borsook so much as saying a word about it. The New York Times profiled her, calling her “The Writer Who Dared Criticize Silicon Valley.” It’s like what a friend once told her: The universe isn’t done with you yet.

Publishers were now keen to get the book back in circulation. That day in December, five of them had sent their bids to her agent. (Eventually, Borsook would settle on Tin House, which published a new edition of Cyberselfish in mid-September, with a foreword by Durán.) The offers were validation, after all those years in the wilderness. Things were finally looking—

“It really kind of broke my heart in so many ways,” Borsook was saying now at the restaurant, as we waited to order. Her mind was back in 2001, wondering again what had happened to her career. Was it something she’d written? Could it have been an actual blacklist? Was it something as depressingly commonplace as sexism? “I really hate playing that card,” she said, “but I do have to wonder.” She just couldn’t figure it, even still, all these years later. In a way, the happy turn of events in the past few months had left her even more discombobulated. As she told me more than once, “I don’t know how to think about myself anymore.” She’d won me over in a matter of hours—a common enough phenomenon, I would learn, among people who find themselves in Borsook’s orbit. When I dropped her off that afternoon, I promised—only half in jest—to find the guy who killed her career.

Ok, but first I have to tell you about Dick Pick. Literally his name. Richard A. Pick. Went by Dick. It was the 1960s, and back then you could walk around with a name like that and no one would think to laugh, even if you were, as Dick Pick apparently was, something of a serial flirt.

Dick Pick was a software developer for a military contractor during the Vietnam War. The story goes that the Army needed a way to track spare parts for Lockheed’s Cheyenne attack helicopter. Alongside his business partner, Don Nelson, he came up with a database operating system that they called—and here you have to imagine two of the shit-eatingest grins you’ve ever seen—the Generalized Information Retrieval Language System: GIRLS. (What, you thought tech bros were a new phenomenon?) Like a lot of tech innovation underwritten by defense spending, GIRLS was soon put to commercial use. Eventually it came to be known as PICK, and it was with this latter name that the operating system found itself under the fingertips of one Paulina Borsook, an employee at a small software company in Marin County.

Before she became one of the sharpest media observers of early Silicon Valley, Borsook first learned how to see tech. That happened in the early 1980s, in front of one of those so-called minicomputers that were in fact big enough to be buried in. The company was called Construction Information Systems, and Borsook was doing some technical writing, documenting in the plainest language she could muster how the software worked.

She learned two important things at that job. The first is that tech is “infrastructure, not magic,” she wrote in a 2015 essay. The second is that the computer is a way of seeing into the mind of another human. It is, ineluctably, social. “Learning about PICK,” she wrote, “taught me that software was a human artifact; that is, I began to be able to think the way the creators of PICK thought … The dyer’s hand, the design sensibility, the cognitive blind spots: all evident and all human artifacts. Technology is idiosyncratic like the humans who devise it and the people who make it are just people.”

Everything Borsook would later write as a journalist covering the industry—the frisky pieces for Salon and Suck, the weightier profiles for WIRED, every barbed word of Cyberselfish—seemed to flow from a simple imperative drawn from her experience at that minicomputer: never lose sight of the human in the machine, the Dicks (as it were) behind the system. Once, she described her writerly voice as one of “agonized humanism,” and that’s it exactly. She was appalled by those in the industry who were determined to leave the human behind. “The most virulent form of philosophical technolibertarianism is a kind of scary, psychologically brittle, prepolitical autism,” she wrote in an especially pungent passage in Cyberselfish. “It’s an inability to reconcile the demands of being individual with the demands of participating in society … these technolibertarians make a philosophy out of a personality defect.”

Her own politics ran to the left, broadly speaking, though like a lot of political commentators of her time she seemed to cherish her own à la carte apostasies. She wasn’t embarrassed to say she agreed with the libertarians in their premises. More than anything she, too, wanted “to be left alone,” she wrote in Cyberselfish. But what Borsook brought to her journalism was an understanding of Silicon Valley as a social creation. Some of that can be attributed to growing up in Pasadena during the space-age boom. She remembers the “vaguely New Deal mentality” of the engineers and scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Caltech, all of them beneficiaries of robust state investment in the war machine. In a place like that, there could be little mistaking the public’s role in the development of new technologies. Thus did Borsook receive an early inoculation against the basic fetishism that would come to define the culture of Silicon Valley—the idea that the power of technology is inherent and not derived from the social relations that produced it.

We shouldn’t overstate things. Not everyone who lived or worked in the shadow of the military-industrial complex drew the same lessons about the virtues of government. In his indispensable 2006 book From Counterculture to Cyberculture, Fred Turner reminds us that the research laboratories spun up during the Second World War were also sites of freewheeling collaboration across disciplines, liberated (so it seemed) from hierarchy—sites of what today we might call disruption. And believe it or not, all those earnest poindexters with their slide rules offered an organizational model for the libertarian communalists of the following era. This was the milieu that would eventually spawn the magazine you have in your hands now. When Borsook began writing for WIRED in the 1990s, it was something of a collision between two very different ways of understanding the political economy of the American midcentury.

Borsook grew up precocious and miserable, the daughter of “infanticidal” parents from whom, at one point, she sought legal emancipation. In 1968, when she was 14 years old, Borsook was shot in the head with a .45 Colt at a distance of 6 feet. She’d been with a couple of girlfriends, and one of them had fired the gun. The official story, the one they gave the cops, was that it was an accident, just dumb kids horsing around. The real story, as Borsook would tell it in 2013, as part of an art installation she called My Life as a Ghost, is that the friend had taken the gun out of a kitchen drawer—it was the friend’s house, and the friend’s parents were Birchers—and started waving it around. Borsook took cover behind the wall in another room. After a moment she popped her head out to see what was happening. Her friend pulled the trigger. Borsook remembers two things: a ringing, pulsing sound, and then silence. The bullet had ripped through her cheek and left through the back of her neck.

Borsook has no doubt the shooting was “accidentally on purpose,” some violent fugitive impulse escaping the tangle of teenage love-hate. She tells the story now without self-pity or sentiment, simply as a way of explaining why her brain works the way it does. Even in the moment, she refused any histrionics. She went to the kitchen and poured cold water on the hole in her face, told her friends to call the operator, and then somehow gave them to understand that now was the time to get their stories straight.

“I felt protective” toward the friend who shot her, Borsook explains now. “I know she immediately regretted it. And I said we need to come off as like we’re just a bunch of ditzy teenagers, as opposed to these alarmingly precocious, kind of scary young women that we were.” She says she refused to cooperate with any attempt to prosecute her friend. The two remained close for years.

It was the jolt from the impact, Borsook believes, that caused the most lasting damage. The effects soon began to present themselves. “That gunshot prematurely aged my brain,” she said in her presentation for My Life as a Ghost. She continued: “I flunked calculus three times and I had no idea why this happened. Ever after, I simply could not process texts of a certain density, such as a geology textbook or a legal opinion. It all washes out. My brain just cannot process and retain quantitative transactions and language of a certain abstraction—all of which are necessary to function as a symbolic-manipulator in a knowledge economy.” (It isn’t just an issue of cognitive function. She says her lifelong environmental sensitivities—so acute now that she can’t even wear a metal watch—were likely exacerbated by the shooting.)

Borsook got a degree in psycholinguistics from UC Berkeley, but even then, communication of any kind was difficult, an issue that predated the shooting. Whether in her speech or her writing, she had a tendency to be “gnomic,” “elliptical,” “highly condensed”—her words. “How my friends put up with it, I don’t know,” she says. She developed a conversational habit, still obvious today, of rounding off her sentences by asking if what she had just said made any sense. “I began to realize that a lot of the ways I think and speak about things don’t make sense to a lot of people,” she says, “so I have to check in with them.” She was still chatty, and nothing would seem outwardly amiss. But she knew something had fritzed out in her head. “Parts of my brain just shut down forever,” she tells me. “Does that make sense?”

One thing that helped, oddly enough, was the technical writing. “Imagine if your hands were really palsied,” she says, gnarling her fingers in front of her face. That’s what it was like in her head, all the words gone stiff and useless. But the precision and clarity required of technical writing forced Borsook to work at her sentences, to limber them up, until ordinary readers could grasp them. The technical stuff certainly had no long-term effects on her prose style—her writing for popular audiences, zippy and full of late-gonzo neologisms like “el stewpido” and “our fabu hyper-accelerated crashboombang economy,” was never, ever plain. To listen to her explain it, the change was more akin to rebuilding an atrophied muscle. She had rehabilitated the capacity to make herself legible to other people. “I could just feel things sort of unkinking,” she says, relaxing her fingers and pulling them from her face. “It was like Jane Fonda aerobics.”

She moved over to the technical end of journalism not long after, joining the staff of Data Communications magazine. That’s where Katie Hafner met her in 1984. Hafner had come on as the news editor; Borsook was the new products editor. The work was impenetrably abstruse. “I have to set the scene for you,” says Hafner, who went on to have a distinguished career in tech journalism. “Paulina was a psycholinguistics major at Berkeley. I was a German literature major at UCSD. This guy Peter Schmader [the managing editor] was some kind of philosopher. The two copy editors, Sue and Sandy, were also English-major people. And we were all complete fish out of water.”

Hafner was immediately taken with Borsook: “She was like the smartest, grumpiest person I’d ever met. And I was in total awe. I’d never met anyone like her. So blunt, completely honest, had something trenchant to say about absolutely everything around her.” Once Hafner set her up with a friend. “They went on a date, and the next day he was just furious,” she recalls. “And he said, ‘Your friend, she has a lot of opinions about everything.’ And I said, ‘Oh, yeah, what’s wrong with that?’”

It was Borsook’s brain that Hafner “worshipped.” She had the right phrase for anything. Hafner remembers a piece Borsook wrote about a chocolate shop in Berkeley in which she described customers who would arrive just after close and “piteously rap on the windows.” Hafner loved the phrase so much she used something like it in a story of her own, in The New York Times. There was the time the two of them went clothes shopping, and Borsook said, “Oh, are you like me—you’re like a sausage with a string tied around the middle?” Hafner laughs. “That is indelibly etched in my head.” When Hafner was living in Berlin, Borsook visited and stayed with her. Hafner paid her friend the highest of compliments a writer could ever receive, from a fellow writer, no less: She asked Borsook to read one of her short stories aloud, as a bedtime story.

The event was in San Francisco, and it was about women and the internet. This would’ve been sometime in the 1990s—Borsook can’t remember when or where, exactly. The commercial internet was in its infancy, and for all its promise of scrambling the dominant gender paradigms, it was also proving to be a fantastic means of shoring them up.

This was also true of the communes in the late ’60s and early ’70s, the ones that gave rise to Stewart Brand’s Whole Earth Catalog and eventually to WIRED itself—the men up front, leaders of the utopia, and the “women in the back having babies and putting bleach in the water to keep people from getting sick,” as Turner has put it. But computer work had belonged to women before it was regendered, in the span of a generation, from a type of clerical job to the domain of the charismatic autonomous man. Nowhere was that more evident than in the media dedicated to covering Silicon Valley. At the talk there were some 30 women in attendance. When they were asked if they read WIRED, they all raised their hands. “And when they were asked if they hated WIRED,” Borsook wrote in an essay, “they all raised their hands.”

The piece appeared in a remarkable anthology from 1996, Wired Women: Gender and New Realities in Cyberspace, published by Seal Press, a sort of consciousness-raising meeting in book form. One of the anthology’s editors, Elizabeth Reba Weise, stops short of saying it was the first book to examine the experience of women online, but it was certainly one of the early ones. “We called it cyberspace, for God’s sake,” Weise says—that’s how early this was. Over and over the contributors, a mix of academics and journalists and women working tech jobs of one kind or another, emphasize that the computer and the internet are tools for women, a way of enabling communication and connection—the gendered division of labor coming to roost now in the differing ways of being online. From Weise’s intro: “In my circle, computers aren’t fetish objects, but tools.” From Ellen Ullman’s essay: “We use the Internet as a tool, like the phone or the fax, a way to transmit news and make appointments.” Susan Clerc: “Like the TV and VCRs, the home computer is a tool that lets her participate fully in the community.” And Borsook: Women “generally are interested in the utilitarian value, not fetish-worthiness, of tools.” The Australian feminist Dale Spender has a pithy old line about computers that is applicable here: “Women use them, whereas men fall in love with them.”

WIRED from its start in 1993 was a magazine for falling in love with computers. Digital utopianism was the order of the day. One of the magazine’s founding editors, John Battelle, today calls the mindset a “naively optimistic libertarianism.” There were more circumspect voices in tech media—in particular the inspired and unjustly forgotten Processed World, which viewed computers from the perspective of the people who had to work with them. In 1995, a British magazine called Mute published an essay, “The Californian Ideology,” that laid out a “critique of dotcom neoliberalism” similar in some ways to Borsook’s. A decade earlier, Lenny Siegel and John Markoff published The High Cost of High Tech: The Dark Side of the Chip, an early criticism of Silicon Valley. Alongside the media were tech-dubious movements, like the mostly memory-holed Neo-Luddites of the 1990s, not to be confused with the new Neo-Luddites. But the critics weren’t breaking through. Processed World’s cofounder, Chris Carlsson, characterizes the era as “an unbelievable frenzy of boosterism and back slapping, we’re all getting rich, ha ha ha, isn’t this great, here, have another line, come to this fancy dinner, here’s a glass of champagne. Oh, you don’t want to be part of the party? Get the fuck out of here.”

In her essay for Wired Women, Borsook reviewed every issue of the magazine to that point and ran the numbers. “Women were the subject of about 15 percent of WIRED articles and only one cover out of twenty-five as of June 1995,” she reported. “There are vague in-house grumbling intimations by women on staff of likely accomplished females being shot down as article-subjects in WIRED editorial meetings and of no-account off-point numb-nut guys being celebrated instead—but that’s par for the course in any mostly-male arena.” She was even more dismayed to find that only 15 percent of WIRED authors to that point were women. One month, she was the only woman on the masthead.

Borsook had been writing for WIRED more or less from its inception. She’d bailed out of Data Communications at the end of the ’80s and had gotten her MFA at Columbia, and now she was making a go of it as a freelancer. One Friday in 1993, she emailed the magazine’s cofounder, Louis Rossetto, a self-styled radical libertarian, asking if he’d be interested in her fiction. Her agent mailed over her MFA thesis, whose concluding novella was a story about an affair that unfolds over email, in all the “perversions and evasions” of what was then a newish medium. It was smart and allusive and full of finely observed shifts in interpersonal weather. By Monday, as Borsook tells it, she was a contributor to WIRED. “Love Over the Wires” appeared in the magazine’s fourth issue.

In short order she was writing big-ticket features. There were profiles of super networker Esther Dyson and Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen. While an ethos of tech utopianism pervaded, writers were allowed to roam with their prose, and Borsook’s touch was unmistakable in her stories. She called Allen “a nerd nonpareil, resembling nothing so much as a manatee with dancey blue eyes.” He was apparently upset with the description, Hafner recalls. “And Paulina, she was so funny. She said, ‘But it’s really sweet! They’re really big and gentle!’”

The pieces weren’t necessarily critical of the tech world, not in the way that Cyberselfish would be, but neither did they go in for gooey panegyrics to the likes of Newt Gingrich, WIRED’s cover boy in August 1995. Despite the plum assignments, Borsook never felt like she belonged. In her Wired Woman essay, she describes herself as a token for the “editorial boykings” of the magazine. “If one is not interested in participating in circle-jerk exercises and paying homage to the alpha male of the moment,” she wrote, “what is there left to do at WIRED?” She bickered with Kevin Kelly, WIRED’s founding executive editor, over a section in her Dyson profile in which she addressed how gender might have shaped her subject’s career. She’d been surprised by how many people asked her, in the course of her reporting, about Dyson’s dating life—surprised as well by the “personal quality of what her detractors had to say,” the snide stuff about her clothes and manners. Kelly, in Borsook’s telling, didn’t think it was relevant. They went back and forth. The section stayed in. (Kelly remembers a narrower dispute. He writes in an email: “My recollection was that she was asking Dyson if she was gay/lesbian and she wanted to report Dyson's response [which I think was ‘negative’], and I thought it was all immaterial to Dyson’s contributions.”)

“I mostly want to be left alone to do my work, to get at that still silent voice within, and not be fighting ideological battles my editors at WIRED might not even consciously realize they are engaging in,” Borsook wrote. “Progress means exchanging one set of problems for a more interesting set of problems—but my struggles with WIRED have been generating problems of ever-decreasing interest. I strive to have other, better, more rewarding and less stupid battles to fight.”

“I always had a fondness for Paulina,” says Battelle. “I mean, I generally have a fondness for difficult people. Like most of my good friends are extremely difficult people. I never was like, ‘Oh, this woman, oh my God, now I’ve gotta deal with her.’ I enjoyed working with her. And yeah, it was difficult. And I did feel like she seemed to sort of arrive besieged, you know?”

Battelle says he “got the sense she didn’t completely buy into some of the core premises and values” of WIRED in that era. He goes on: “She was very critical of the political philosophy that was evident in the magazine.”

In a sense, Cyberselfish is a continuation of Borsook’s criticisms of early WIRED. In the mid 1990s, her agent, Stuart Krichevsky, started pitching the book around under the pulpier title Deadly Embrace, a computer science term for when processes get stuck because each is waiting for another to release a resource. (It became Cyberselfish after Mother Jones published an essay by Borsook under that headline.) Nothing about it came easy. A deal with WIRED’s publishing arm fell apart after Borsook gave an interview in which she recited some of her criticisms of the magazine. Another publisher proved a bad fit. Eventually, Lisa Kaufman at PublicAffairs rescued Cyberselfish from publishing oblivion, and the book landed just as the dotcom bubble began to deflate.

If sales were modest, the book was “a reputational success” for the publisher, Kaufman says. The New York Times sang its praises. Turner goes so far as to call it “the first actual from-the-left critique of the tech world that I’m aware of” and “one of the first clear articulations of some of the really nasty conflicts that are built into some of the cybercultural thinking of the period.” He adds: “The thing that Paulina got right off the bat: She just saw right through that, all the way through. She saw that these firms were commercial firms. They were seeking market positions. They were seeking standing.”

Not everyone had such glowing reviews. Battelle, broadly sympathetic to the book’s premise, recalls thinking Cyberselfish was a “pretty thin deconstruction” of tech libertarian utopianism. One tech journalist recalled similar grouching among colleagues about the lack of reporting, by which they presumably meant investigative legwork. Cyberselfish was full of reporting in the most basic sense—conversations over dinner, dispatches from conferences, information gleaned from others and related to readers—but it was all of the “soft” variety, cultural and thus dismissible.

The work dried up after the book came out—though it was drying up for a lot of people in the first decade of the new century. Borsook couldn’t seem to catch anyone’s eye. She wrote an essay for Processed World in 2001 on “the disappeared of Silicon Valley,” about failure in the time of the dotcom boom, the piece itself a narrative of Borsook’s own failure to write the story she had set out to tell. She tried other subjects. Borsook was sure she could scare up some interest in a story about a grassroots campaign she was working on, Stop the Spray, which was agitating against the use of pheromone pesticides in the Bay Area targeting the light brown apple moth. Nothing. For a time she lived as an Airbnb superhost in return for free rent. All her worst suppositions about not belonging were being confirmed. “The universe is just telling me to go jump off a pier,” as Borsook puts it.

Maybe she was catastrophizing—or maybe catastrophe was just a normal state of affairs for her. “There was always this sort of Calamity Jane thing about Paulina,” Hafner says. “She’d go through stuff, and you’d go, ‘Oh, my gosh.’” She would go on a work trip, and someone would break into her room and steal her prized watches. Or she would show up to the office one day with an enormous bandage on her leg, the victim of a burst hot-water bottle. “I just thought, how does this woman endure what she endures?” Hafner says.

Could an actual blacklist have been among her torments? I put the question to a number of people.

John Battelle, who was gone from WIRED by the time Cyberselfish came out: “I think it’s conceivable. Whether or not it’s factual, I can’t speak to … WIRED was a quasi-religious community. And while we were OK with people debating fundamental principles of the community, we weren’t OK with people, you know, with ad hominem attacks. My sense is if someone kind of wasn’t on the WIRED train, then, you know, they’re not gonna be invited to write for the magazine. That doesn’t strike me as an unusual thing.”

Gil Durán, whose angry thread on Bluesky helped kick-start the Borsook revival: “It’s likely. At the same time, one of the ways you get blacklisted in journalism is just nobody’s interested in you, right? Doesn’t have to be a conspiracy or something. As we’ve seen, there was not much of a hunger for real criticism of tech in Silicon Valley. “

Katie Hafner: “I would lean heavily on the side of there was no conspiracy. She was grumpy. She didn’t want to write suck-up stories, which was a lot of what was happening back then. That doesn’t mean she was blacklisted. It’s just that she had a lot of opinions.”

Steven Levy, longtime contributor to WIRED: “I’d push back against the word blacklist—especially [given] the connotations of it, the horrendous things of the McCarthy era. It may very well be that what she was pushing in the core of her writing was an unpopular theme which now people see maybe there was something to it, but back then led to people thinking, we don’t have an appetite for that kind of story.”

John Markoff, tech reporter for the Times until 2016: “There are stories people don’t want to hear. It wasn’t so much about Paulina but that the things she wanted to write didn’t have a market.”

Hafner again: “It was just because she’s Paulina. I mean, it’s hard to be Paulina.”

“I don’t even know if the blacklist existed,” Borsook was saying. “I don’t think it existed.” This time I was the one who’d brought up her years in exile. We were sitting in the shade in her friend’s backyard in Berkeley. It was August, and she was waiting to be photographed for this very magazine, the one that had handled her roughly for a time and then, maybe worse, had decided not to handle her at all. The new edition of Cyberselfish was no longer notional. The paperback had arrived in the mail that day, and when she pulled it out of the padded envelope and held that damn book up, it was as if she were displaying an award. Her agent, Stuart Krichevsky, told me that when the Tin House offer came in, Borsook practically squeaked.

“I—this sounds weird—I don’t think TDB was important enough to be blacklisted,” Borsook said. She had come to see her own exile as part of a larger process. No conspiracies or blacklists were needed to render her disposable. “It was such a changed media landscape,” she said. It was more than the media, too. From the vantage of 2026, Cyberselfish reads a little like Borsook’s account of her own encroaching obsolescence—she was describing a campaign, ultimately successful, to root out a whole way of understanding tech. There could be no seeing the dyer’s hand, no perceiving the Dicks in the system, not in the utopia the technolibertarians were building for us.

Earlier we had been talking about ghosts, the way they seem to pop up in different corners of the story Borsook tells about her life. Even before her friend had shot her, she had this spectral sense of herself, a compulsive feeling of not belonging that only heightened with the violence done to her brain. “Hmm, maybe I really am not supposed to be here,” as she put it in 2013, “and my life ever since has been an accident.” She was standing on a deck now, white hair blowing this way and that in the wind, white scarf wrapped around her neck. A photographer was snapping away, an assistant holding up a bounce board, redirecting daylight toward Borsook’s face. A strange but happy image suggested itself to me: an old ghost in a warm sun.

Does that make any sense?

entries.title: 16 Products From Women Designers You Need to Know
entries.summary: From electric trucks to health trackers, women designers are guiding consumer tech to a better place.
entries.content:
Slate Auto Fastback SUV

Tisha Johnson is a rarity in the car world: an automotive design leader who is not a man. Women are sometimes put in charge of the interiors or the materials, but few get to shape the whole look of a vehicle. As head of design at the EV-maker Slate, Johnson does. The pickup truck version of its EV starts at just under $25,000, making it the cheapest pickup on sale in the US, electric or not. Trouble is, cheap products are usually a compromise, and compromises rarely inspire affection. Johnson’s Slate, however, has won design awards, not just praise for its price tag.

“We didn’t want [Slate] to be a jerk,” Johnson says, “or look like a beast on the road.” That thinking shows in the truck itself—not just in its modular, add-on-friendly design (pictured here in its Fastback guise), but in the fact the EV was designed to be loved. Strong shoulders and approachable round headlamps were favored over macho arrowed surfacing. “The attraction that draws you to Slate is based on something that is lasting from inside out. It’s a deeper connection,” Johnson says. Some 180,000 reservations and counting for the Slate, along with those awards, seem to more than prove her point.

Away The Carry-On: Aluminum Edition

Away was founded in 2015 by entrepreneurs Jen Rubio and Steph Korey, both with backgrounds at the eyewear maker Warby Parker. In its first year, Away generated $12 million in sales and sold more than 100,000 stylish, reasonably priced suitcases. It has been an impressive rise, and the Softside Carry-on currently tops WIRED’s best buy list. Here however, we’ve chosen the aluminum version of the company’s handsome roll-aboard that’s built tough but perfectly sized for the overhead bin. It has a 32-liter capacity, dual TSA locks, 360-degree wheels, and an internal compression system. The signature hidden laundry bag remains a brilliant accoutrement.

Jelenew Mont Blanc Ultralight Long Windproof Jacket

Cofounded by six-time cycling world champion Marion Clignet, Jelenew combines female-specific articulated shaping, recycled nylon, mesh ventilation and an adjustable hem in a windproof shell that packs into a 6.3 x 9.8-inch bag. Clignet brought elite racing experience directly into the brand’s development, with the fit shaped around women’s proportions rather than scaled down from men’s clothing. This particular jacket uses 94 percent recycled nylon, a PFAS-free water-repellent treatment, UV protection, and mesh ventilation. Generous waist pockets and adjustable drawstrings add practical detail.

TaylorMade Kalea Gold Driver

Light, easy to launch, and forgiving, Kaela has been designed for women who want more performance than they can get from hacking a set of men’s clubs. Principal product-development engineer Michelle Penney helped lead the development of the range, with input from female TaylorMade employees, players, and and dedicated women’s advisory board. The final design takes into account the key differences in women’s swing profiles. The 460 cc carbon driver is 44 inches long, with 11.5- or 13.5-degree lofts and a lightweight 47-gram shaft intended to help generate speed without making the club harder to control.

Natural Cycles NC° Band

Cofounded by CERN physicist Elina Berglund Scherwitzl, who helped discover the Higgs boson, Natural Cycles makes the world’s first FDA-cleared birth-control app. Its screenless NC° Band syncs its health readings to the app. Wear it on your wrist while you sleep and it tracks your temperature, heart rate, and movement during the night, then automatically syncs all that data to your phone in the morning. Those numbers are fed into the app’s algorithm to give you accurate—Natural Cycles claims an impressive 93 percent accuracy—daily fertility guidance. A recently announced Whoop partnership helps strengthen both brand’s offerings too.

Adafruit Pimoroni Badgeware Badger

Ladyada, aka Limor Fried, became the first female engineer to appear on the cover of WIRED in April 2011, just six years after she founded Adafruit from her MIT dorm room. Her alias was inspired by 19th-century English mathematician and computing pioneer Ada Lovelace, which in turn provided inspiration for the brand’s name. Fried has grown Adafruit into a 100 percent woman-owned force in open-source electronics, making components, tools, and educational kits that lower the barrier to coding and hardware hacking. The company’s range spans beginner-friendly boards, wearable controllers, and touchscreens, alongside quirky maker gear such as the pictured programmable, wearable e-paper name badge.

Raide Women’s TrailTech Cargo Tank

More than just another running top, this multifunctional design combines an unpadded sports bra, a vest, and much of the carrying capacity of a small hydration pack in a single 4.6-ounce layer. Five well-positioned pockets hold up to 30 fluid ounces of water, a phone, your rain shell, and up to six fuel gels, all while keeping the load close to your body to help minimize bounce. Laser-perforated chest panels add ventilation, and the fit is designed around female anatomy rather than adapted from a men’s cut. It is a neat solution for runners who want to go the distance without adding layers on layers.

Vacheron Constantin Overseas Self-Winding

There was a time, not so long ago, when all serious timepieces had two clear traits. They were massive—we’re talking over 48 mm here, which fine if you have Schwarzenegger-sized forearms but useless for those who don’t—and they were aimed just at men. Women’s watches would have comparatively basic mechanical movements, or be quartz powered and covered in jewels.

Thankfully, general watch size trends have swung back the other way, and now small- and mid-size pieces are very much in demand. This means women with a serious eye for horology now have some truly excellent choices. This new Vacheron is a perfect example: Clocking in at 34.5 mm, this Overseas will suit both men and women very well in either stainless steel or pink gold. It’s a nearly exact shrunken version of the 41 mm model, and nothing has been dropped in the downsizing apart from the outer seconds track on the dial. The quick-release bracelet, two extra quick-change straps, 40-hour power reserve, and sapphire caseback are all present.

Dreame Miracle Pro

AI is drying hair now, or more specifically, adjusting temperature, heat, and airflow automatically. Dreame’s dryer also includes a conditioning essence atomizer and red light therapy to take extra care of your scalp. The 1,400-watt dryer monitors temperature 1,000 times per second to keep the airflow ultra consistent. The dryer also comes with four magnetic attachments: nozzles for styling, smoothing, and defrizzing, plus a diffuser. Snap one on, and the Miracle pro senses which one you’ve attached and adjusts the dryer’s power and heat for the best possible results.

Music Man St. Vincent HHH

Annie Clark, aka art-rocker St. Vincent, sketched the original shape for her signature guitar using angles that combine midcentury retro-futurism with the bold triangular tuxedo worn by avant-garde performer Klaus Nomi. She then worked through around 20 prototypes to get the weight, balance, and feel for the design just right. Despite the sharp lines, the body is heavily beveled with an exceptionally narrow waist, and Clark explicitly designed it to sit comfortably against a woman’s torso. Built from lightweight okoume wood, it weighs around 7.5 pounds, with a roasted maple neck that offers easy access to the upper frets (where the shredding happens). The three custom DiMarzio mini-humbuckers are controlled by a five-way selector.

KiwiCo STEM Kits

Chemical engineer and mother-of-three Sandra Oh Lin founded KiwiCo to make hands-on science, engineering and creative projects fun, practical, and easy to tackle at home. It offers kits for babies, kids, teens, and adults, with age-appropriate builds (and yes, we wouldn’t be surprised if the kids’ stuff was more advanced than the adults’) ranging from simple sensory play and mechanical grabbers to animatronics, marble roller coasters, and working desk lamps. Available individually or by subscription, everything that’s needed to build each device arrives in the box, with clear instructions and explanations of the ideas behind each project.

IDA Helia Pro

Informed by biometric data from professional women soccer players, IDA builds high-performance boots around women’s feet, combining specific fit with lightweight materials. Cofounder Laura Youngson started the company after seeing how poorly existing boots served women players. The Helia Pro packs in the tech with a lightweight mesh upper, a highly responsive soleplate made from Pebax thermoplastic, and a soft foam insole. There are also female-specific flex zones throughout the shoe, and shorter, rounded cleat studs laid out in a unique pattern that’s designed for firm ground and artificial grass.

New Balance Fresh Foam Cremorne Toe Safety Shoe

Looking closer to a pair of trail runners than conventional safety footwear, these are proof you don’t need to be clodhopping around in heavy boots to stay protected on the job site. The composite toe guards shield your piggies from impacts without the weight of steel, an anti-perforation layer protects the sole of your foot, and a reinforced heel support adds stability when you’re lifting loads. Its grippy outsole is designed for wet, slick, or oily floors, and offers antistatic protection while also being able to withstand temperatures of at least 572° Fahrenheit for 60 seconds. The shoes borrow foam cushioning and a springy polyurethane insert from New Balance’s athletic footwear to make long shifts easier on your feet.

Circular Smart Ring 3 Slim

We’re not quite at the point where smart rings are indistinguishable from jewelry, but the gap is closing. At just 1.9 grams, and with a noticeably slimmer profile than the second-generation model, Circular’s Ring 3 Slim blends in well, yet still tracks sleep, heart rate, blood oxygen level, skin temperature, daily activities, and heart-rate variability. It now adds NFC for contactless payments and practical vibration alerts and alarms. There’s also a larger Ring 3 Pro, which adds FDA-cleared electrocardiogram sensors for detecting signs of atrial fibrillation. Blood-pressure trends and glucose insights are planned for a later update.

Posedla Joyseat 3.0

Finally, a saddle that actually fits. Posedla sends an at-home imprint kit, then uses sit-bone measurements, riding position, and algorithmic modeling to 3D-print bespoke padding precisely profiled for your posterior. The resulting Joyseat is not merely made in a chosen width. Its shape and stiffness are individually generated too, using a custom TPU lattice rather than stock foam. Width can be specified from 130 to 170 mm in one millimeter increments, and Joyseat will also take into consideration the bike you use and what sorts of riding you do—whether you’re a racer, a weekend tourer, a bike camper, or a long-haul commuter.

Liv EnviLiv Advanced Pro 0-AXS

Bonnie Tu, chair of the company behind Giant bikes, founded Liv after struggling to find bikes that fitted properly. Liv designs from women’s biometric data, giving every frame size its own geometry, then applies its findings to a collection that includes city, gravel, commuter and elite bikes like the EnviLiv Advanced Pro. Its carbon frame, handlebars and stem are shaped using computer modelling and wind-tunnel testing to reduce drag, while 50 mm-deep carbon wheels and SRAM Force AXS wireless electronic gears complete the race-ready build. More importantly, fit is treated as a complete system, with stem length, handlebar width, crank length and saddle choice all selected to suit the rider rather than added later as generic components.

entries.title: The 34 Best Gifts for Dads (2026)
entries.summary: Dads are typically tough to shop for. Let me help with these WIRED-tested gift ideas.
entries.content:
It occurs to me that, as a new(ish) father, and someone who reviews products for a living, I am a nightmare to get gifts for. I’m not alone. Most of my friends have no idea what to get their dad, and end up brainstorming in group chats with anyone they can get their hands on.

Fear not, I’m here to make gifting a little easier this year (or at the very least, contribute to the brainstorm). Below are some of the best WIRED-tested gifts for the dad or father figure in your life, including travel gadgets, dad-approved apparel, and best-in-class earbuds. I’ve personally gifted a few of these to my dad, with great results.

Updated September 2026: I completely overhauled this guide with 27 new picks, including tech accessories, headphones, dad-approved apparel, fitness gear, and more.

For the Travel Dad

For the Music-Loving Dad

If Dad loves to host large get-togethers, parties, or tailgates, this portable party speaker is one of the loudest, most durable I’ve tested. It’s got a clean, understated, loudspeaker-slash-rock-concert look that’s a far cry from the light-show techno vibes of most portable party speakers. It’s very durable, with large silicone balls on each corner for impact protection. Plus, it has a swappable battery. I honestly wouldn’t be surprised if it outlasts most other speakers in his collection. You can learn more in my full Soundboks Rider review.

Dad-Approved Apparel

For the Outdoor Dad

I can’t think of many dads who don’t love an electric bike. The Letric XP4 750 isn’t just one of WIRED’s top electric bike picks, it’s one of the best-selling electric vehicles in America, ranking third behind the Tesla Model Y and Model 3 in 2024. WIRED reviewer Michael Venutolo-Mantovani says it only took 20 minutes to assemble and lasted well over 50 miles of riding on a single charge. This version has an upgraded 750-watt motor that helps tackle hillier terrain than the original.

For the Car Dad

I didn’t think I needed a tiny portable vacuum (I have a perfectly good cordless vacuum), but I was gifted this tiny Hoto vacuum years ago, and it has been endlessly useful. I use it to clean strollers, keyboards, my desk, you name it. It’s small and portable enough to take anywhere you need a quick clean. I gifted one to my brother-in-law, and he uses it to clean his car constantly—it basically lives in his car’s glove compartment.

For the Foodie Dad

This is the best pizza oven for the dad who doesn’t have space for a full-sized outdoor one. It’s an indoor electric pizza oven that can fit on a countertop, and can heat to up to 850 degrees Fahrenheit. Like all of the brand’s appliances, it’s easy to use, so it's more fun than work to make that fan-favorite pizza just right.

For the Dad Who Is a Kid at Heart

The Lego DeLorean Time Machine from the Back to the Future trilogy is the perfect centerpiece for any movie buff, but Great Scott, it’s $200. A better alternative is the version from Lego’s Speed Champions series. It’s much cheaper and easier to build (pick either the original with lightning hook or the “future” upgrade with Mr. Fusion and hover wheels), but it has the same charm and display quality. It comes with Doc Brown and Marty McFly Minifigures, but sadly, it won’t hit 88 miles per hour.

For the Fitness Dad

These are my favorite open ear headphones for anyone, not just Dad. Because they leave your ears open, you can easily hear the world around you, along with your music. That’s why I love them for outdoor runs and bike rides. This premium model uses a mix of bone conduction (think vibrations) and air conduction (think tiny speakers pointed toward your ears) to deliver sound that’s clearer than most smaller open earbuds. You can learn more in our full Shokz OpenRun Pro 2 review.
